analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run health insurance plan to compete with private insurers on the new exchanges.
analysis.headline: The bill to add a public health insurance option drew 76 Democratic cosponsors but never got a hearing; it sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee from January 2011 until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the 2010 health care law to create a public health insurance plan, run by the Department of Health and Human Services and sold through the new insurance marketplaces starting in 2014. The plan would have to follow the same rules as private plans, charge premiums that cover its own costs, and start with payment rates set at Medicare levels — plus a 5 percent bonus for doctors and other providers in the first three years. The goal was to give people buying coverage a cheaper alternative to private insurers and force more price competition into the marketplaces.
analysis.who_benefits: People buying health insurance on the exchanges — including people who would newly buy coverage there — would get a government-run plan option designed to be low-cost, which could also push private insurers to lower their own premiums to compete. The bill specifically requires the plan to be offered nationwide and to work to reduce racial and ethnic health disparities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People buying coverage on the exchanges

how_it_helps.text: Requires HHS to offer a public health insurance plan through the exchanges starting in 2014, with the Secretary's primary responsibility to create a low-cost plan without compromising quality or access.
The public plan must follow the same rules on benefits, provider networks, consumer protections, and cost sharing as private plans on the exchanges, and it may only be sold through the exchanges.

Premiums must be set to fully finance the plan's health and administrative costs, and the $2 billion in start-up funding must be repaid to the Treasury over ten years — so the plan is designed to be self-financing rather than a permanent drain on taxpayers.

The plan would pay doctors and hospitals at Medicare rates for 2014-2016, with a 5 percent payment bonus for participating providers, and could use innovative payment methods like accountable care organizations and bundled payments to hold down costs.
Medicare's fraud-and-abuse rules, including the False Claims Act, would apply to the plan, and enrollees would get the same access to federal courts that Medicare beneficiaries have.

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would face a government-backed competitor on the exchanges, likely losing customers and pricing power. Hospitals and doctors would be paid at Medicare rates, which are generally lower than what private insurers pay, though softened by a 5 percent bonus in the first three years. The Treasury would front $2 billion in start-up money plus 90 days of claims reserves, which the plan must repay over a decade.

drawbacks.text: Starting payment rates at Medicare levels would pay doctors and hospitals less than commercial insurance does; the bill tries to soften this with a 5 percent bonus for 2014-2016, but critics of the original public option argued Medicare-level rates shift costs onto privately insured patients instead of reflecting real efficiency.

The bill caps its own cost-control ambition: payment rates after 2016 may not exceed what the Medicare-rate model would have produced, but the plan must still fully finance itself through premiums, so any shortfall in rural or high-cost areas would show up in higher premiums for that plan's enrollees.
The plan is available only inside the exchanges, so people who get insurance through an employer — the majority of insured Americans — would not be able to choose it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people shopping on the exchanges, the bill offered a concrete way to add price competition and a low-cost plan option, with the plan required to cover its own costs and repay its start-up funds. The real costs fall on insurers, hospitals, and doctors through lower revenue, and honest supporters had to answer the objection that Medicare-level payment rates could shift costs onto the privately insured rather than producing genuine savings. The exchange-only design also limits how many people could ever choose it. On balance it was a meaningful but targeted change, not a universal coverage expansion.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, then to its Health subcommittee a month later, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lynn Woolsey of California introduced the Public Option Deficit Reduction Act on January 5, 2011, the opening day of the 112th Congress.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce; on February 1, 2011 it was referred further to the Subcommittee on Health.
Seventy-six House members cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats.
No further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no vote — was recorded for the rest of the 112th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers came out ahead: the low-cost public competitor the bill would have placed on the exchanges never reached the market, and they kept the exchange business to themselves. Hospitals and physicians also avoided the Medicare-level payment rates the bill would have set. The roughly 40-plus million uninsured Americans and exchange shoppers who could have used a cheaper plan option gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Lynn Woolsey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 112th Congress and recruited 45 original cosponsors from the Congressional Progressive Caucus wing of the party.

for.name: 76 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the public option bill, including senior members like George Miller, John Conyers, Barney Frank, and Jan Schakowsky.

against.name: Rep. Fred Upton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it was sent to the Health subcommittee and stayed there for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 76 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill died in a committee run by the Republican House majority without any recorded opposition vote — no Republican ever supported it.

industries.note: The bill would have placed a government-run plan, built on Medicare rates and low overhead, alongside them on the exchanges — a direct competitor for customers and pricing power. Insurers avoided it entirely because the bill never advanced. [S3]

Medicare providers would automatically be in the plan's network unless they opted out, and would be paid Medicare rates plus a 5 percent bonus for 2014-2016 — more patients, but lower per-service payment than commercial insurance. Their interest in higher payments runs against the public's interest in lower premiums. [S3]

Prescription drugs not covered under traditional Medicare would be paid at rates the HHS Secretary negotiates directly, rather than the list prices that dominate commercial coverage. The bill never got far enough for this to matter. [S3]
